title: Heat, temperature and expansion
summary: Learn about temperature, heat, specific heat, changes of state, heat transfer and expansion.
cards.0.p: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles. As tea heats up, its particles move faster. Temperature does not depend on the amount of matter. A boiling drop and a boiling bucket of water are both at 100 °C.
cards.0.key: Temperature is not an energy. It is a measure of average energy, and you measure it with a thermometer.
cards.1.p: Heat is energy transferred from hot to cold because of a temperature difference, so an object does not contain heat. Internal energy is the total energy of the particles, and it depends on the amount. The unit of heat is the joule (J) or the calorie.
cards.1.svg#0: Heat: from higher to lower temperature,
cards.1.svg#1: not from larger to smaller internal energy
cards.1.key: Heat flows from higher temperature to lower temperature, not from larger internal energy to smaller.
cards.1.once.soru: You put a cold spoon into hot tea. Which way does heat flow?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.yazi: From the tea to the spoon
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: Heat is energy transferred from hot to cold because of a temperature difference.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.yazi: From the spoon to the tea
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: A cold spoon does not heat the tea. Heat always flows from hot to cold.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: Heat flows as long as the temperatures are different.
cards.2.p: A thermometer uses the fact that a liquid expands when it heats up. At 1 atm, water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C. Kelvin and Fahrenheit values come from T = t + 273 and F = 1.8·t + 32.
cards.2.key: As a temperature difference, 1 °C = 1 K = 1.8 °F. The Kelvin scale has no negative values, and 0 K is about −273 °C.
cards.3.p: This difference is called specific heat (c). Specific heat is the heat that raises the temperature of 1 g of a substance by 1 °C. The specific heat of water is 1 cal/g·°C, larger than that of most substances. The heat absorbed is Q = m·c·ΔT.
cards.3.key: Specific heat identifies a substance. Heat capacity depends on mass, so it does not identify one.
cards.4.p: When objects at different temperatures touch, heat flows until the temperatures are equal. This is called thermal equilibrium. If no heat is lost to the surroundings, heat gained equals heat lost.
cards.4.key: The equilibrium temperature lies between the two starting temperatures. For the same substance, it is closer to the temperature of the larger mass.
cards.4.etk.soru: Mix hot water with water at 20 °C. No heat is lost. Both are water, so c is the same.
cards.4.etk.ciktilar.1.ad: Heat gained by the cold water
cards.5.h: Changes of state and latent heat
cards.5.p: When a pure substance changes state at constant pressure, the heat it absorbs goes into overcoming the attraction between particles, and the temperature does not change. The heat needed is Q = m·L (L: heat of fusion or vaporization).
cards.5.svg#4: red: absorbs heat · blue: releases heat
cards.5.svg#7: temperature is constant during a change of state
cards.5.key: Melting 25 g of ice at 0 °C takes 25 × 80 = 2000 cal. The water that forms is still at 0 °C.
cards.6.p: The temperature-time graph of ice heated at constant power looks like steps. On the sloped parts the temperature rises (Q = m·c·ΔT). On the flat parts the state changes (Q = m·L).
cards.6.key: On a flat part, heat is absorbed and internal energy rises, but the temperature stays constant.
cards.6.etk.soru: What happens on each part of the heating curve?
cards.6.etk.noktalar.0.acik: On this sloped part, Q = m·c<sub>ice</sub>·ΔT. The specific heat of ice is small, so this line is steep.
cards.6.etk.noktalar.1.acik: On the flat part at 0 °C, the heat absorbed (Q = m·L<sub>fusion</sub>) overcomes the attraction between particles, and the temperature does not change.
cards.6.etk.noktalar.2.acik: On this part, Q = m·c<sub>water</sub>·ΔT. The specific heat of water is large, so the line is less steep.
cards.6.etk.noktalar.3.acik: On the flat part at 100 °C, Q = m·L<sub>vaporization</sub>. The heat of vaporization is larger than the heat of fusion, so this flat part is longer.
cards.6.etk.noktalar.4.acik: Once all the water has turned into steam, the temperature rises again.
cards.6.once.soru: You heat ice at constant power. What does the temperature-time graph look like while the ice melts?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: While it melts, the heat absorbed goes into the change of state. The temperature stays constant and the graph goes flat.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: The temperature does not rise until the melting is over.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: The temperature of ice that absorbs heat does not fall.
cards.7.h: Is any ice left in the mixture?
cards.7.p: Is any ice left? Compare the heats. If the heat the water can give off while cooling to 0 °C is not enough to melt all the ice, the equilibrium is at 0 °C and some ice remains.
cards.7.svg#0: 100 g of ice at 0 °C + 200 g of water at 20 °C
cards.7.svg#3: needed to melt all the ice
cards.7.svg#6: equilibrium at 0 °C; 50 g of ice left
cards.7.once.soru: You drop 100 g of ice at 0 °C into 200 g of water at 20 °C. The water gives off 4000 cal while cooling to 0 °C. Melting all the ice takes 8000 cal. What happens in the end?
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: 4000 cal melts only 50 g of ice (L = 80 cal/g). The equilibrium is at 0 °C and 50 g of ice remains.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: That would take 8000 cal. The water can give off 4000 cal at most.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: To freeze, the water must give off heat, but the ice is at 0 °C and cannot absorb that heat.
cards.8.p: Evaporation happens at any temperature, at the surface. The fast particles escape, so the liquid cools. Boiling happens at a specific temperature, with bubbles throughout the liquid. When the outside pressure drops, the boiling point drops too.
cards.8.key: Impurities lower the freezing point and raise the boiling point. That is why salt is spread on roads in winter.
cards.8.once.soru: After sweating, you feel cold in the wind. Why?
cards.8.once.secenekler.0.neden: During evaporation the fastest particles escape. The sweat left behind and your skin cool down.
cards.8.once.secenekler.1.neden: Wet skin feels cold in a warm wind too. The real cause is evaporation.
cards.8.once.secenekler.2.neden: Sweat is at body temperature. What cools you is its evaporation.
cards.9.p: In conduction, heat passes from particle to particle, and metals conduct well. In convection, a heated fluid rises and carries the heat. In radiation, heat travels as waves, even through empty space. Air and wool insulate.
cards.9.key: In a thermos, the vacuum reduces conduction and convection, and the shiny surface reduces radiation.
cards.9.once.soru: In the same room, a metal door handle feels colder than a wooden table. Why?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: Both are at room temperature. Metal draws heat from your hand quickly, so it feels cold.
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.yazi: The metal is at a lower temperature
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: In the same room both are at the same temperature. The difference is in conduction.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: Wood does not produce heat. It just conducts heat slowly.
cards.10.h: What does the rate of conduction depend on?
cards.10.p: The heat conducted increases with a larger temperature difference and cross-sectional area, and decreases with greater thickness. The material matters too. For example, copper conducts heat much better than glass.
cards.10.svg#7: k: thermal conductivity of the material (large for copper)
cards.10.once.soru: If the outer wall of a house is made thicker, what happens to the heat escaping through it?
cards.10.once.secenekler.0.neden: The heat has to be conducted along a longer path. As thickness increases, the heat conducted decreases.
cards.10.once.secenekler.1.neden: A thick wall conducts less heat, not more.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: The heat conducted depends on thickness, and a thick wall holds the heat in.
cards.11.p: A heated solid gets longer, and the change in length is ΔL = L₀·λ·ΔT. λ is the coefficient of linear expansion, and it identifies the material. For steel, λ is about 1.2·10−5 1/°C. An object that cools gets shorter.
cards.11.svg#4: steel rail: L₀ = 10 m, ΔT = 40 °C → ΔL ≈ 4.8 mm
cards.11.key: The change in length is directly proportional to the original length and to the temperature change.
cards.12.p: A heated plate expands in every direction (ΔA ≈ A₀·2λ·ΔT), and a hole in it gets bigger too. Liquids expand more than solids, and gases expand the most.
cards.12.svg#3: every part of the plate expands
cards.12.key: A container filled to the brim overflows when heated, because the liquid expands more than the container.
cards.12.once.soru: You heat a metal plate with a hole in the middle. What happens to the hole?
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.neden: The plate expands in every direction. The edge of the hole also stretches outward, and the hole gets bigger.
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.neden: Intuition says so, but every part of the plate gets longer, including the edge of the hole.
cards.12.once.secenekler.2.neden: The edge of the hole is metal too, and it expands.
cards.13.p: As water warms from 0 °C to 4 °C it contracts, and its density is greatest at 4 °C. Surface water that cools sinks to the bottom. In the end the surface freezes, and water at 4 °C stays at the bottom.
cards.13.key: When water freezes, its volume increases by about 9%. That is why pipes and rocks crack in winter.
cards.13.once.soru: When a lake freezes in winter, where does the ice form?
cards.13.once.secenekler.0.neden: Water is densest at 4 °C, and surface water that cools sinks to the bottom. The surface reaches 0 °C last and freezes. The ice insulates, and living things survive beneath it.
cards.13.once.secenekler.1.neden: Ice is less dense than water, so it cannot stay at the bottom.
cards.13.once.secenekler.2.neden: Water close to 4 °C stays at the bottom. Freezing happens at the surface.
cards.14.p: In summer, wires sag and bridge joints narrow. A bimetallic strip is made of two metal strips with different expansion coefficients. When heated, it bends toward the metal that expands less, and it is used as a switch in thermostats and irons.
cards.14.key: Hold a stuck metal jar lid under hot water. Metal expands more than glass, and the lid loosens.
cards.14.once.soru: A stuck metal jar lid opens easily after you hold it under hot water. Why?
cards.14.once.secenekler.0.neden: The heated metal lid expands more than the glass rim and loosens.
cards.14.once.secenekler.1.neden: Hot water does not melt glass.
cards.14.once.secenekler.2.neden: Metal does not soften at this temperature. It just gets a little bigger.
cards.15.p:
• Temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy, and heat is energy that is transferred.
• T = t + 273 and F = 1.8·t + 32.
• Heat is Q = m·c·ΔT, and Q = m·L during a change of state.
• At thermal equilibrium, heat gained equals heat lost.
• The change in length is ΔL = L₀·λ·ΔT, and water is densest at 4 °C.
quiz.0.q: In a container with no heat loss, 100 g of water at 90 °C is mixed with 200 g of water at 30 °C. What is the equilibrium temperature in °C?
quiz.0.e: Heat gained equals heat lost: 100·(90 − T) = 200·(T − 30). This gives T = 50 °C. The equilibrium temperature is closer to that of the water with the larger mass.
quiz.1.q: Ice at −20 °C is heated at constant power at 1 atm until it turns into steam. Put the stages in order.
quiz.1.ogeler.0: Ice warms, its temperature rises to 0 °C
quiz.1.ogeler.1: Ice melts, the temperature stays at 0 °C
quiz.1.ogeler.2: Water warms, its temperature rises to 100 °C
quiz.1.ogeler.3: Water boils, the temperature stays at 100 °C
quiz.1.ogeler.4: Steam warms, its temperature rises above 100 °C
quiz.1.e: On the sloped parts the temperature rises (Q = m·c·ΔT), and on the flat parts the state changes (Q = m·L). In order: the ice warms, it melts, the water warms, it boils, and the steam warms.
quiz.2.q: Match each event with the concept that explains it.
quiz.2.ciftler.0.0: The handle of a pot on the stove getting hot
quiz.2.ciftler.1.0: Warm air rising in a room
quiz.2.e: In the metal handle, heat is conducted from particle to particle. Heated air rises and carries heat by convection. The Sun's heat arrives through empty space by radiation. As sweat evaporates, the fastest particles escape and the skin cools. Heated wires expand and get longer.
quiz.3.q: A metal plate with a circular hole in the middle is heated. How does the diameter of the hole change?
quiz.3.e: A heated plate expands by the same ratio in every direction, like a photograph being enlarged. The hole grows just as it would if it were filled with metal.
quiz.3.y.0: The plate does not expand inward. It expands proportionally in every direction. The rim of the hole also gets longer, and the hole gets bigger.
quiz.3.y.2: There is no material in the hole, but the metal around it expands. The edges of the hole move away from each other.
quiz.3.y.3: Expansion is a steady growth from start to finish. The hole never gets smaller first. It keeps getting bigger.
A:ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Set the thermometer, heat water and iron, melt ice and expand a rail.
A:adimlar.0.metin: At 1 atm, a boiling drop of water and a boiling bucket of water are both at 100 °C. Internal energy is the sum of the energies of all the particles.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: Which one has the larger internal energy?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The temperatures are equal, so the average energy is equal. But internal energy is a total, not an average.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The average energy is the same, but the bucket has far more particles. Internal energy is a total, so it depends on the amount of matter. Temperature does not.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The drop has very few particles. Total energy grows with the number of particles.
A:adimlar.1.metin: On the Kelvin scale, you find the temperature by adding 273 to the Celsius value. Set the thermometer to 300 K.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: 300 − 273 = 27 °C. On the Fahrenheit scale this is 1.8 × 27 + 32 = 80.6 °F.
A:adimlar.2.metin: 100 g of water and 100 g of iron are placed on identical heaters. Each will absorb the same amount of heat, 1000 cal. Both start at 20 °C.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Water has a very large specific heat. So the same heat warms it only a little.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The masses and the heat are equal, but the substances are different.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Heating 1 g of iron by 1 °C takes about 0.11 cal, while 1 g of water takes 1 cal. The same 1000 cal warms the water by 10 °C and the iron by about 91 °C.
A:adimlar.3.metin: 200 g of water at 80 °C is mixed with cold water at 20 °C. Find the amount of cold water that brings the mixture to 44 °C.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.tamam: 200·(80 − 44) = 7200 cal was given off, and 300·(44 − 20) = 7200 cal was absorbed. There is more cold water, so the equilibrium is closer to 20 °C.
A:adimlar.4.metin: There is 10 g of ice at 0 °C, and the heat of fusion of ice is L = 80 cal/g. Melt all the ice, but do not warm the water.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.tamam: It takes 10 g × 80 cal/g = 800 cal. The temperature stayed at 0 °C throughout the melting. Any heat supplied after this warms the water.
A:adimlar.5.metin: There is a 6 mm gap between 10 m steel rails, and for steel λ is about 1.2·10⁻⁵ 1/°C. Raise the temperature and find the moment the gap just closes.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.tamam: 10 000 mm × 1.2·10⁻⁵ × 50 = 6 mm. On a hotter day the gap is not enough and the rails buckle. That is why gaps are left between rails and expansion joints are built into bridges.
A:kapanis.0: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles, and it does not depend on the amount of matter. Heat is energy transferred from hot to cold.
A:kapanis.1: The Kelvin value is T = t + 273, and the Fahrenheit value is F = 1.8·t + 32.
A:kapanis.2: When there is no change of state, the heat absorbed is Q = m·c·ΔT, and a substance with a large specific heat warms slowly. At thermal equilibrium, heat gained equals heat lost.
A:kapanis.3: During a change of state, the heat absorbed is Q = m·L, and the temperature stays constant.
A:kapanis.4: A heated solid gets longer, and the change in length is ΔL = L₀·λ·ΔT.
